items.text: Work Email Missing on Your Mac? This Could Be Why
items.article: If your work email on your Mac isn't syncing today, it might well have to do with Microsoft's cut-off of Exchange Web Services (EWS). As of October 1, 2026, Microsoft began switching off EWS by default in Exchange Online. If you haven't heard of it before, EWS is the aging protocol that Apple's Mail and Calendar apps still use to sync Microsoft 365 work accounts. The cutoff has been signposted for a while. Microsoft stopped adding new features to EWS back in 2018, while in 2023 the company announced that it would start disabling the protocol in Exchange Online from October 2026. It's being described as a phased rollout, so some users may be impacted sooner than others. For those affected, system admins can still turn EWS back on, but only until April 1, 2027, when it shuts down for good. Apple says that it is "actively working with Microsoft" to move its Mac apps over to the newer Graph API in a macOS 27 update. That update has yet to arrive, but it surely won't be long before it does. In the meantime, Outlook for Mac works just fine, and iPhone and iPad users won't be affected because they use Exchange ActiveSync rather than EWS. Get weekly top MacRumors stories in your inbox.

Hawaii’s iconic Hōlei Sea Arch has collapsed into the Pacific Ocean, disappearing just days after visitors were still photographing the landmark. The 90-foot arch at Hawaii Volcanoes National Park on the Big Island was standing firm Wednesday, Sept. 23, but was gone by Sunday night, according to the National Park Service . Officials do not know exactly when the tourist attraction fell and suspect it may have happened while the park was temporarily closed for three days during Tropical Storm Nolo . Nolo brought heavy rain and powerful winds to the Big Island last week, triggering flash flooding and road closures. Visitors were warned to stay away from the site near Hōlei Sea Arch, where the cliffs drop straight into the Pacific and can collapse without warning.

items.text: Look inside: Luxury Kinsale penthouse with sea views for €3.25m
items.article: Airy and spacious three-bed built on the site of a former Mercy Convent in popular west Cork location Imagine waking up in a penthouse and walking to the balcony outside your bedroom. Below you is the sea and in the distance, bobbing sail boats. A new luxury penthouse, built on the site of a former Mercy Convent in Kinsale , Co Cork , could afford you this experience. One of four apartments called Schooner Cove, the last of 30 to be built in a complex called Avila, the penthouse takes up the entire top floor of the former convent and offers incredible views. Developed by Cumnor Construction, the project is a far cry from the former Convent of Mercy and school, which formerly occupied the site. It opened in 1845 with 700 pupils and six Mercy Sisters at the start of the Irish famine. The convent and industrial school closed decades ago, and the school, convent, chapel and gardens were later sold. The three-bedroom penthouse, which spans 297sq m (3,200sq ft), was designed by JCA Architects. Airy and spacious, with high ceilings and elegant original columns, its rooms are differentiated by smoked-glass panel doors. Its large open-plan kitchen/dining/sittingroom opens to a terrace with sea views. The furnishings rely mostly on muted tones of grey, taupe, beige and blue, which combine well with its minimalist design and futuristic-style light fittings. One of the most striking aspects of this apartment is the large original sash ecclesiastical windows in the sittingroom space.

items.article: The seaside town has a lot of fans, but I'm not one of them It's rare to head to the Scottish Highlands and leave feeling underwhelmed. Across my 34 years, I've clocked up well over a year in Scotland's western mountains, and like everyone, I've fallen for plenty of the region's corners. There's the impossibly tranquil and beautiful village of Glenelg, tucked away from the world's pressures on the far side of the Mam Ratagan Pass. Follow the coast a little further and you'll reach Sandaig, a shore of pure white sand with scallops bubbling in the shallows, which inspired Gavin Maxwell to write 'Ring of Bright Water'. If you only have an afternoon and want to soak up as much Highland scenery as you can, it's hard to beat a trip on the West Highlands Line. This railway, once named the world's most beautiful, carries you over moorland, around lochs and through mountain passes, and only Switzerland can really compete.
